flawed_step: Step 1—the claim that every finite unit-distance graph is 3-colorable—is false. No supporting numbered proof steps are supplied, and the explicit seven-point graph below contradicts the claim.
counterexample: Let x=(0,0), a=(sqrt(3),0), p=(sqrt(3)/2,1/2), q=(sqrt(3)/2,-1/2), b=(5sqrt(3)/6,sqrt(33)/6), r=((5sqrt(3)-sqrt(11))/12,(sqrt(33)+5)/12), and s=((5sqrt(3)+sqrt(11))/12,(sqrt(33)-5)/12). The following pairs are exactly distance 1: xp,xq,ap,aq,pq; xr,xs,br,bs,rs; and ab. For the first five pairs, the squared distances follow immediately from 3/4+1/4=1. For the second group, put u=(5/6,sqrt(11)/6) and n=(-sqrt(11)/6,5/6); then u and n are perpendicular unit vectors, b=sqrt(3)u, r=(sqrt(3)/2)u+n/2, and s=(sqrt(3)/2)u-n/2, proving all five distances are 1. Finally, |a-b|^2=(sqrt(3)/6)^2+(sqrt(33)/6)^2=1. In any proper 3-coloring, p and q have different colors, so their common neighbors x and a must both receive the third color. Likewise, r and s have different colors, forcing x and b to have the same color. Hence a and b have the same color, contradicting the unit edge ab. Thus the unit-distance graph induced by these seven points is not 3-colorable.
assessment_summary: The seven explicit points form a finite unit-distance graph containing two diamond subgraphs whose 3-color constraints force the endpoints of the unit edge ab to have the same color. Therefore the first clause, and hence the stated conclusion under the supplied convention, is false.
